questions.q: Excavators at a mound in the Indus basin find three layers. Top: a gateway with a water-filled ditch outside it, and silver punch-marked coins. Middle: mud huts and clay pots, with no drains and no large buildings. Bottom: planned streets with a drainage system and rows of specialised craftspeople's workshops. A guide says, 'This place has always been a city.' Which reading fits the chapter?
o: A Harappan city, then a long spell of village life, then a walled Second Urbanisation city
A city that stayed urban throughout, with the huts being the poorer quarters of the same city
A village that grew into a Harappan city and was then given up for good by its people
Two cities of the Second Urbanisation, separated only by a short pause while it was rebuilt
questions.a: The bottom layer has Harappan components (drainage, specialised workshops), the middle layer shows people reverting to a village lifestyle once those components had gone, and the top layer (fortified gateway, moat, coins) belongs to the later urban phase. So the guide's 'always a city' is wrong.

questions.q:
A university can fund the excavation of only one of two mounds. Its aim is to learn about the millennium in which, the chapter says, urban life was largely absent after the Harappan urban order ended (take that order as ended about 1900 BCE). Mound P (Indus basin): surface finds of hut floors, clay pots and farm tools, dated about 1500 BCE. Mound Q (Ganga plains): a visible gateway with a water-filled ditch, and a Buddhist text that names the town, dated about 600 BCE.
(a) Which does each mound's evidence show: village life after the First Urbanisation, or the Second Urbanisation?
(b) Work out how many years after 1900 BCE each mound's date falls, and say which one lies inside the chapter's 'whole millennium' without urban life.
(c) The chapter says excavations confirmed the urban centres that literature describes. What would digging Mound Q add to what its text already gives?
(d) Decide which mound to dig, using your answers to (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) P shows village life after the First Urbanisation (the urban components are missing); Q shows the Second Urbanisation. (b) P: 1900 - 1500 = 400 years, inside the millennium (1900 to 900 BCE); Q: 1900 - 600 = 1300 years, outside it. (c) Physical confirmation that the centre the text describes really existed. (d) Mound P: the aim is the millennium without urban life, and only P falls inside it, whereas Q lies after it and its text already tells us it was a city; digging Q would confirm a known urban centre but would not answer the stated aim.
s: Part (a): P is village life after the First Urbanisation; Q is the Second Urbanisation
Part (b): 400 years (inside the millennium) and 1300 years (outside it)
Part (c): excavation would confirm that the centre the literature describes really existed
Part (d): chooses Mound P and justifies it with the dates from (b) and the stated aim

questions.q: A student finds that a walled town in the Ganga plains is dated about 700 BCE and a town in the far south about 400 BCE, and says, 'The book says the Second Urbanisation began everywhere together, so one of these dates must be wrong.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: It began in the Ganga plains and nearby regions and spread, so a later southern date is expected
The book says the southern towns appeared first and the north followed, so the Ganga-plains date is the one to doubt
The book says every region became urban at the same time, so both dates should be moved to the same century
The book says the Ganga plains were never part of the Second Urbanisation, so the 700 BCE town cannot belong to it
questions.a: The book says the new phase began in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions, gradually spreading to other parts; southern cities began emerging from about 400 BCE. So a Ganga-plains town at 700 BCE and a southern town at 400 BCE fit together, and the student's quoted claim is not what the book says.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A site whose only layer is a village of mud huts dated about 1500 BCE cannot be counted as part of the Second Urbanisation.
Reason (R): The chapter places the Second Urbanisation in the 1st millennium BCE, and 1500 BCE falls in the 2nd millennium BCE, which comes before it.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R gives the date reason: the book puts the new urban phase in the 1st millennium BCE, and 1500 BCE (2nd millennium BCE, counted backwards) is earlier; the site is also a village, not an urban centre.

questions.q: A timeline in the chapter covers 1900 BCE to 300 BCE, with marks at 1900, 1200, 800, 400 and 300 BCE. (a) Which two neighbouring marks are closest together, and how many years apart are they? (b) Take the Harappan urban order as ended at 1900 BCE. The chapter says urban life then stayed absent for a whole millennium. Which marks on this timeline fall inside that millennium?
questions.a: (a) 400 BCE and 300 BCE, 100 years apart (the other gaps are 700, 400 and 400 years). (b) The millennium runs from 1900 BCE to 900 BCE, so only the 1200 BCE mark falls inside it; 800 BCE, 400 BCE and 300 BCE come after it.
s: Part (a): 400 and 300 BCE, 100 years apart
Part (b): the millennium ends at 900 BCE, so only 1200 BCE falls inside it

questions.q: Archaeologists list four finds from different layers: a public drainage system, an iron ploughshare, a punch-marked silver coin and a street of specialised craft workshops. Which pair of finds, found together in one layer, would place that layer in the Second Urbanisation and not in the Harappan phase?
o: The iron ploughshare and the punch-marked silver coin
The public drainage system and the punch-marked silver coin
The public drainage system and the iron ploughshare
The public drainage system and the street of craft workshops
questions.a: The chapter ties iron metallurgy and the first use of coins to the Second Urbanisation, while a sanitation system and specialised occupations belong to the Harappan urban order. Only the ploughshare and the coin are both marks of the later phase.

questions.q: Three towns are described as busy in late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts. Excavators have uncovered a moat and gateway at Town 1, have dug one trench at Town 2 and found nothing yet, and have not dug at Town 3. Which statement best fits what the chapter says about our evidence?
o: Town 1 has both kinds of evidence, Town 3 the texts alone, and one empty trench at Town 2 settles nothing
Towns 1 and 3 are equally certain, since the literature is full of references to all three towns and that is enough
Town 2 shows that the texts were wrong, since a real urban centre would have left a moat in its first trench
None of the three can belong to the Second Urbanisation, since only Harappan sites have been excavated
questions.a: The book names two sources: excavations that confirmed the centres, and the literature describing them. Town 1 has both, Town 3 only the texts, and one empty trench at Town 2 does not disprove a city the literature describes.

questions.q: A classmate's timeline entry reads: 'c. 1900 BCE - Harappan cities fade. The very next century - cities rise in the Ganga plains.' Using the chapter's time frame, show that this entry cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says urban life remained absent for a whole millennium, about ten times longer than one century, so the Ganga-plains cities rose about a thousand years later.
s: States the gap the book gives: a whole millennium without urban life
Compares: next century is only 100 years against about 1000
Concludes the cities of the Ganga plains belong to the 1st millennium BCE, long after the break

questions.q: Rohan says: 'After the Harappan cities were abandoned, there was no town anywhere in India until the Second Urbanisation began.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Not fully. The book says urban life was largely absent but there may have been a few towns here and there in north India, and important regional cultures existed.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the absolute claim
Reason: urban life was largely, not totally, absent for about a thousand years
Evidence: a few towns may have existed in north India and regional cultures continued

questions.q:
The history teacher of a Pune school shows a chart of a site called Kheda. Layer 1: a planned town with a drainage system, abandoned around 1900 BCE. Layers 2 to 4: only huts and farm tools, with people living there without a break until about 900 BCE. Layer 5: a gateway with a water-filled ditch outside it, and an ancient text that names the place. The students must write one caption for the whole chart.
(a) Work out the break in town life shown by the chart, say which phase Layer 5 belongs to, and say whether the break fits the chapter's figure.
(b) A student says, 'Layers 2 to 4 show that the people of Kheda vanished.' Use the chapter's account of some Harappan cities to correct this.
(c) Layer 5 gives two kinds of evidence for a city of the later phase. Name both and say which one the dig itself supplies.
(d) Choose a caption, 'Kheda: the city that vanished' or 'Kheda: a place where life never stopped'. Give one change that makes your chosen caption fit the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 1900 - 900 = 1000 years without a town; Layer 5 is the Second Urbanisation; it matches the chapter's whole millennium. (b) The chapter says in some cities people continued living there but reverted to a rural or village lifestyle; what vanished was urban life, not the people. (c) Ancient literature (the text) and archaeological excavation (the gateway and ditch); the dig supplies the excavation evidence. (d) Either caption is acceptable only with a qualifying change: 'vanished' becomes 'urban life vanished' and 'never stopped' becomes 'life never stopped, but as village life for about a thousand years'.
s: Part (a): 1000 years; Second Urbanisation; fits the whole millennium
Part (b): people stayed on but reverted to a village lifestyle; urban life, not the people, vanished
Part (c): literature and excavation; the dig gives the excavation evidence
Part (d): picks a caption AND makes one qualifying change; an unqualified choice earns no mark

questions.q: A student argues: 'The Second Urbanisation also began partly in the Indus basin, so the Harappan cities never really ended.' (a) Use the chapter's account of the time between the two phases to answer her. (b) Name the other main region, besides parts of the Indus basin, where the chapter says the new phase began.
questions.a: (a) Sharing a region does not make them one continuing story: the Harappan urban order disintegrated, its components disappeared and urban life stayed largely absent for about a thousand years before the new phase began. (b) The Ganga plains.
s: Part (a): the Harappan order disintegrated and urban life was largely absent for about a millennium, so the later phase is a new one
Part (b): the Ganga plains

questions.q:
Match each find in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A grinding stone and mud-hut layer from the millennium after Harappa  2. A Jain text describing a busy city  3. A gateway dug up with a moat outside it  4. Urban life that, the book says, has continued right up to today
Column II: a. Literary evidence for the Second Urbanisation  b. Village life after the First Urbanisation  c. Archaeological confirmation of an urban centre  d. The Second Urbanisation as the book describes it
questions.a: The hut layer shows village life after the First Urbanisation; the Jain text is literary evidence; the excavated gateway is archaeological confirmation; and the book says the Second Urbanisation has continued right up to today. Swapping the text and the dug-up gateway is the usual slip.

questions.q: Take the Harappan urban order as ended in 1900 BCE. If urban life stayed absent for the length of time the chapter gives, and the first fortified gateway of the new phase was then built 150 years after that, the gateway dates to about ___ BCE.

Read the statements.
Statement 1: The Harappan cities were abandoned in the 1st millennium BCE, just before the Second Urbanisation began.
Statement 2: A mound with a Harappan layer followed by a layer of huts is consistent with the chapter's account of what happened to some Harappan cities.
Statement 3: A Ganga-plains town named in a late Vedic text and also yielding a dug-up moat is supported by two kinds of evidence.
Which statements are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the Harappan order disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE, about a thousand years before the new phase. Statements 2 and 3 agree with the chapter (some people stayed on in a village lifestyle; literature plus excavation are the two sources).

questions.q: A writer says: 'The Harappan civilisation and the Second Urbanisation are one long story of urban life in India; calling the later one ‘Second’ is a mistake.' Using the chapter, judge this claim: say how far it is right and how far wrong.
questions.a: Partly right, mostly wrong. Right: both are phases of Indian urban life, the later one began partly in the Indus basin, and a few towns and important regional cultures may have existed in between. Wrong: the Harappan components (structures, markets, specialised occupations, writing, sanitation, administration, a ruling class) disappeared, people who stayed lived a village life, and urban life was largely absent for about a thousand years; the later phase began in the 1st millennium BCE mainly in the Ganga plains, so it is rightly counted as a second one.
s: Verdict: partly right, but the 'one story' claim fails
Right part: both are urban phases; a few towns and regional cultures may have continued in between
Wrong part 1: the urban components of the Harappan order all disappeared and people reverted to village life
Wrong part 2: urban life was largely absent for about a thousand years
Wrong part 3: the new phase began in the 1st millennium BCE, mainly in the Ganga plains and parts of the Indus basin

questions.q: Write a three-line note for a historian's file that establishes that a particular Ganga-plains city of the 1st millennium BCE really existed. Line 1 must give a literary clue (name the kind of literature), line 2 an excavated clue, and line 3 say why having both is stronger than either alone.
questions.a: Line 1: a late Vedic, Buddhist or Jain text describes the city. Line 2: excavators uncovered its remains, for instance a fortified gateway with a moat. Line 3: the literature describes the centre and the dig confirms that it existed, so each covers what the other cannot.
s: Line 1: names late Vedic, Buddhist or Jain literature as describing the city
Line 2: gives an excavated find such as a gateway, moat or street remains
Line 3: explains that excavation confirms what literature describes (two sources are stronger than one)

questions.q: (a) The chapter puts the Harappan decline in the early 2nd millennium BCE and the Second Urbanisation in the 1st millennium BCE. State which millennium BCE each of the years 1900 BCE and 800 BCE belongs to. (b) A classmate says, 'The 1st millennium comes before the 2nd, so the Second Urbanisation must be the older phase.' Explain her mistake.
questions.a: (a) 1900 BCE is in the 2nd millennium BCE (2000 to 1001 BCE); 800 BCE is in the 1st millennium BCE (1000 to 1 BCE). (b) BCE years count down towards the Common Era, so the 2nd millennium BCE is the earlier one; the Harappan phase is therefore the older and the Second Urbanisation the later.
s: Part (a): 1900 BCE is in the 2nd millennium BCE and 800 BCE in the 1st
Part (b): BCE dates run backwards, so the 2nd millennium BCE is earlier and the Harappan phase is older

questions.q: Excavators report two Harappan sites. Site M has no layer at all above its urban ruins. Site N has a layer of mud huts directly above its urban ruins. (a) Which site fits the chapter's 'abandoned' cities and which fits the cities where people 'continued living there'? (b) What does the existence of both kinds of site tell us about the claim 'every Harappan city was abandoned'?
questions.a: (a) Site M fits an abandoned city; Site N fits a city where some people continued living, reverting to a rural or village lifestyle. (b) The claim is too strong: the chapter says some cities were abandoned, but in others some people stayed on.
s: Part (a): M is abandoned, N is the continued village life
Part (b): 'every' is wrong, since some cities were abandoned and in others people stayed on

questions.q: True or False: 'The Second Urbanisation ended when the mahajanapadas ceased to exist around 300 BCE.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The mahajanapadas ceased to exist by about 300 BCE, but the book says the Second Urbanisation has, incidentally, continued right up to today; it is a phase of urban life, not the life of those states.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the mahajanapadas ended by about 300 BCE, but the Second Urbanisation has continued to today

questions.q: A historian records four finds. Find A: planned streets with a public drainage system, last used about 1900 BCE, Indus basin. Find B: hut floors and clay pots in a layer directly above A, dated about 1500 BCE. Find C: a fortified gateway with a water-filled ditch, dated about 800 BCE, Ganga plains. Find D: a Buddhist text that names the town of Find C as busy. (i) Place A, B and C in the phase or condition they show. (ii) Work out the years from A's last use to C and compare with the chapter's figure. (iii) State what D adds to C. (iv) A student says, 'The town of C grew straight out of the town of A.' Judge this using the finds.
questions.a: (i) A: Harappan urban order (First Urbanisation); B: village life after it; C: Second Urbanisation. (ii) 1900 - 800 = 1100 years, close to the chapter's whole millennium (roughly a thousand years). (iii) D is literary evidence that matches the excavated evidence in C, so C rests on two sources. (iv) Not supported: B shows village life in between, 1100 years separate A and C, and C is in the Ganga plains, a different region; the later town is a new urban phase, not a direct growth of A.
s: Part (i): A is Harappan, B is village life, C is the Second Urbanisation
Part (ii): 1100 years, about the chapter's millennium
Part (iii): D is literary evidence that C's excavated remains confirm (two sources)
Part (iv): rejects the claim, citing the village layer B
Part (iv): also cites the 1100-year gap or the different region

questions.q: A historian wants a find that would show a mound was still an urban centre and had not yet reverted to village life. Which find would NOT help?
o: A hearth with cooking pots and a storage jar inside a one-room mud hut
A street lined with workshops of metalsmiths, potters and weavers beside a busy market lane
A drain running from several houses into a public sanitation system under the street
A large public structure, built in several stages, standing in the middle of the settlement
questions.a: A hearth, pots and a storage jar in a hut belong to ordinary village life. Specialised workshops and markets, a public sanitation system and elaborate public structures are components of the urban order that had disappeared when people reverted to village life.

questions.q: Two neighbouring janapadas, one rich in fertile land and one near hills with iron ore, begin to exchange grain and iron along a new route that links them. Which development does the chapter connect with such growing links?
o: Both grow, and some such states may merge into a bigger unit, a mahajanapada
Each janapada shrinks, as trade draws its people away from the clan territory
Both lose their rajas, as an assembly of traders takes over the rule
Both become capitals with a moat, within a single generation of the first exchange
questions.a: The book says the janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them, and that by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some of those early states had merged into bigger units called mahajanapadas. It says nothing about shrinking, traders taking over, or instant capitals.

questions.q:
The museum in Rajgir, the old capital of Magadha, has Rs 15 lakh to build a full-size model of one feature of a mahajanapada capital. The moat model costs Rs 12 lakh and the narrow-gateway model costs Rs 7 lakh. Information boards for the exhibit cost Rs 6 lakh. The museum's stated aim is to show visitors how the state controlled the movement of people and goods entering the city.
(a) Show that the museum cannot build both models, and work out the money left after the gateway model.
(b) Which feature does the chapter link to controlling movement of people and goods, and what does it say the other feature was for?
(c) The museum's draft board says, 'No capital of the mahajanapadas exists today.' Correct it using the chapter.
(d) Decide what the museum should build, together with the boards, using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 12 + 7 = 19 lakh, which is more than 15 lakh; after the gateway model 15 - 7 = 8 lakh is left. (b) The narrow gateway lets guards control the movement of people and goods; the moat was further defence. (c) The book says most ancient capitals continue to be living cities today, often 2,500 years old. (d) The gateway model plus the boards (7 + 6 = 13 lakh, within 15 lakh): it serves the stated aim of showing control, whereas the moat model with the boards would cost 18 lakh and shows defence, not control.
s: Part (a): 19 lakh exceeds 15 lakh; 8 lakh left after the gateway model
Part (b): narrow gateway for control of people and goods; the moat as further defence
Part (c): most capitals are living cities today, often 2,500 years old
Part (d): gateway model plus boards (13 lakh), justified by the aim and the costs

questions.q: The chapter says that by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some early states had merged into mahajanapadas, and that the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by about 300 BCE. A student takes 700 BCE as the date of the merger and 300 BCE as the end. About how long did the mahajanapadas then last?
o: About 400 years
About 1,000 years
About 700 years
About 100 years
questions.a: BCE years count down, so the span is 700 - 300 = 400 years. Adding the two dates gives 1,000 and quoting the first date gives 700, both common slips.

questions.q: A museum wall has one standard panel for every mahajanapada on the chapter's more frequent list, except the four it names as the most powerful, which each get a double-width panel. Counting a standard panel as 1 unit, the wall needs ___ units.

Match each observation at a ruined capital in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A wide water-filled ditch outside the wall  2. A gateway narrowed to the width of a single cart  3. A busy modern city standing over the ruins  4. An Ashmaka site lying near the Godavari River
Column II: a. Guards could control people and goods entering  b. The capital had further defence  c. Most such capitals are living cities today  d. The mahajanapadas were not all in the Ganga plains
questions.a: The moat is further defence; the narrow gateway is for control of movement; the modern city shows that most ancient capitals are living cities; Ashmaka in central India near the Godavari shows the states were not confined to the Ganga plains. Swapping the moat and the gateway is the usual slip.

questions.q: Group P contains Gandhara, Ashmaka and Anga. Group Q contains Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti. State on what basis the chapter singles out each group, and say what the two groups together show about where the strongest states stood in relation to the edges of the list.
questions.a: Group P marks the extent of the more frequent list: Gandhara in the northwest, Anga in the east and Ashmaka in central India close to the Godavari. Group Q is the set the chapter names as the most powerful new states. Together they show that the strongest states are not the ones at the edges of the list; they lie inside the area the 16 cover.
s: Group P: the ends of the list (northwest, east, central India near the Godavari)
Group Q: named as the most powerful of the new states
Conclusion: the most powerful were not the edge states; the list's reach is wider than its strongest states

questions.q: A student says: 'The mahajanapadas came first; the clans settled into janapadas only after the large states had formed.' Use the chapter's dates to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says clans became associated with janapadas towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, and that by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some of these merged into mahajanapadas, so the order is janapada then mahajanapada.
s: Janapadas were clan territories towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE
Mahajanapadas formed by merging, by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE
So janapadas came first and mahajanapadas later

questions.q: Three students summarise the rise of the mahajanapadas. Dia: 'A clan settled a territory under a raja; as trade networks connected such territories, they grew, and some merged into bigger states.' Eshan: 'All the old texts agree on one list of exactly 16 mahajanapadas.' Farah: 'The mahajanapadas lasted without a break until about 100 BCE.' Judge each student against the chapter, correct every error, and say who is the most accurate.
questions.a: Dia is right: janapadas were clan territories under a raja, they grew as trade networks connected them, and some merged into mahajanapadas; she leaves out the date, by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE. Eshan is wrong: the texts have different lists, and 16 is only the more frequent one. Farah is wrong: the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by about 300 or 200 BCE. Dia is the most accurate.
s: Dia is correct on clans, a raja, trade networks and merger
Adds the date Dia leaves out: by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE
Eshan: the texts give different lists; 16 is the more frequent one
Farah: they ceased to exist by about 300 or 200 BCE, not 100 BCE
Concludes that Dia is the most accurate

questions.q: A student argues that so many mahajanapadas lay in the Ganga plains only because their forts were easier to defend there. (a) Give two of the reasons the chapter itself suggests. (b) Why can she not cite the chapter for her own reason?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: growth of agriculture in the fertile plains, availability of iron ore in the mountains and hills, formation of new trade networks. (b) Easier defence is not among the reasons the chapter gives; it offers several possible reasons 'including' those three, so she may suggest her own, but she cannot cite the chapter for it.
s: Part (a): two of fertile agriculture, iron ore in the hills, new trade networks
Part (b): the chapter does not give easier defence as a reason, so she cannot cite it

questions.q:
Ananya's group in a Kolkata school counts the 16 mahajanapadas of the usual list and finds 10 inside the Ganga plains and 6 outside. The chapter says there may have been a few more mahajanapadas than the list names. The group has time to study only one of the three reasons the chapter suggests for the clustering (fertile agriculture, iron ore in the hills, new trade networks), and the only data it has is a map of old trade routes.
(a) What share of the 16 does the group's count put inside the plains? If two more mahajanapadas, both outside the plains, are added to make 18, what is the share? Give both to one decimal place.
(b) What does the change in (a) show about quoting an exact percentage as the chapter's finding?
(c) Which of the three reasons can the trade-route map speak to, and what does the chapter say trade networks did for the janapadas?
(d) Should the group study the trade reason with the data it has, or wait to collect iron-ore data first? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 10/16 = 62.5 percent; 10/18 = 55.6 percent. (b) The share changes with the list used, and the chapter says the texts give different lists and a few more states may have existed, so only 'many were in the plains' can be claimed, not an exact figure. (c) New trade networks; the chapter says the janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them. (d) Study the trade reason now: it is the one the group has data for and the chapter links it directly to the janapadas' growth; waiting for iron-ore data would use up the time and the chapter itself only says these are possible reasons.
s: Part (a): 62.5 percent and 55.6 percent
Part (b): the share depends on the list; lists differ and more states may have existed, so quote 'many', not an exact percentage
Part (c): trade networks; the janapadas grew as trade networks connected them
Part (d): chooses the trade study and justifies it by the available data and the chapter's link

questions.q: A student writes, 'A traveller in 150 BCE met the raja of Kosala, ruler of one of the sixteen mahajanapadas.' Which comment fits the chapter's dates?
o: The claim is doubtful: the mahajanapadas had ceased to exist by 300 or 200 BCE, before 150 BCE
The claim is sound: the chapter says the mahajanapadas lasted until about 100 BCE
The claim is doubtful: the chapter says Kosala never had a raja at its head
The claim is sound: only the janapadas had ceased by then, while the larger states went on much longer
questions.a: The book says the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by 300 or 200 BCE. A meeting in 150 BCE would fall after that, so the claim is doubtful. The other options invent dates or facts the chapter does not give.

questions.q: A quiz answer reads, 'The chapter proves that every member of a clan spoke one language and followed the same customs.' Which comment fits the chapter's wording?
o: It says clans were only 'probably' sharing a language and customs, so it does not prove this
The chapter says clans were forbidden to share a language, so the answer is the reverse of the truth
The chapter says common customs belonged only to mahajanapadas, never to clans in a janapada
The chapter says the answer is right because each clan was bound to a janapada capital
questions.a: The book says, 'As people formed clans or groups, probably sharing a common language and common customs', so the claim is a likelihood, not a proof. The other options attribute to the chapter statements it does not make.

questions.q: A ruined site now lies under farmland, but it shows a rampart, a moat and a narrow gateway. (a) Which two features of a mahajanapada capital does it match? (b) A student says it cannot have been a capital because the chapter says most capitals are living cities today. Why is that reasoning faulty?
questions.a: (a) The fortification and the moat outside it (and the deliberately narrow gateway). (b) The book says most, not all, capitals continue as living cities, so a site that is now farmland can still have been a capital.
s: Part (a): two features such as rampart or fortification, moat, narrow gateway
Part (b): the book says most, not all, are living cities

questions.q: A student writes, 'The janapadas merged into mahajanapadas in 700 BCE.' (a) Rewrite the sentence to match the chapter's wording. (b) Why does the chapter give a loose date and not a single year?
questions.a: (a) By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, some of those early states had merged together into bigger units called mahajanapadas. (b) The evidence for such remote periods is incomplete (the chapter says so about its sources), so only an approximate time can be given.
s: Part (a): 'by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some of the early states had merged' (not 'all', not one year)
Part (b): the data for remote periods is incomplete, so an approximate date is all the chapter gives

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The usual list of mahajanapadas names 16 states, though the texts give different lists.
Statement 2: Most mahajanapada capitals were fairly large, well-fortified cities with a moat outside the fortifications.
Statement 3: All sixteen mahajanapadas of the usual list lay inside the Ganga plains.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: the list runs from Gandhara in the northwest to Anga in the east and to Ashmaka in central India, so only many, not all, lay in the Ganga plains.

questions.q: A student lists six possible reasons for so many mahajanapadas lying in the Ganga plains: (1) growth of agriculture on fertile land; (2) iron ore in the nearby mountains and hills; (3) new trade networks; (4) a shorter route to the sea; (5) plenty of timber for building ships; (6) a single ruler uniting the plains. (i) Sort the six into those the chapter gives and those it does not. (ii) The chapter introduces its reasons with 'several possible reasons ... including'. What does that wording tell you about how certain historians are? (iii) Which given reason does the chapter tie most directly to the growth of the janapadas, and in what words?
questions.a: (i) Given: (1), (2) and (3). Not given: (4), (5) and (6). (ii) The reasons are possible, not proved, and the list is not complete; the student may suggest others but cannot cite the chapter for them. (iii) New trade networks: the chapter says the janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them.
s: Sorts (1), (2) and (3) as given by the chapter
Sorts (4), (5) and (6) as not given by the chapter
Part (ii): 'possible reasons ... including' means uncertain and not exhaustive
Part (iii): trade networks; the janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them

questions.q: One sentence of the chapter says the most powerful of the new states were Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti. Another says Magadha, Kosala and Avanti were among the most powerful monarchical states. (a) Which of the four is missing from the second sentence? (b) Does the second sentence contradict the first? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Vatsa. (b) No: 'among the most powerful' does not claim to be a complete list, and the second sentence is about states that were monarchies; it does not say Vatsa was less powerful.
s: Part (a): Vatsa
Part (b): no contradiction, since 'among the most powerful' is not a complete list

questions.q: A student says, 'Once the mahajanapadas had formed, not a single janapada was left.' (a) Which statement in the chapter contradicts this? (b) What does that statement suggest about the list of 16?
questions.a: (a) The chapter says there may have been a few more mahajanapadas, along with some smaller janapadas continuing independently. (b) The list of 16 is the more frequent list, not a complete count of every state.
s: Part (a): some smaller janapadas continued independently
Part (b): the 16 is the more frequent list, not a complete count

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rajgir today is a living city, although Magadha, of which it was the capital, ceased to exist as a mahajanapada.
Reason (R): A city must disappear as soon as the state of which it is the capital ceases to exist.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: A is true: the chapter calls Rajagriha 'modern-day Rajgir' and says the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by 300 or 200 BCE. R is false: most ancient capitals continue to be living cities today, often 2,500 years old.

questions.q: The chapter opens with Kautilya's advice that the kingdom be protected by fortifying the capital and frontier towns, that the land sustain its people (and outsiders in a calamity) with cultivable land and mines, that it not depend only on rain for water, and that it have good roads and waterways. Which site would he recommend for a capital?
o: A fortified town on fertile land with mines, good roads and waterways, and water not reliant on rain alone
A fortified town on fertile land with few roads, whose water depends only on the rain
A well-watered fertile town with good roads and waterways, but no fortification at the capital or the frontier
A fortified town with good roads and mines on land that could not feed its people in a calamity
questions.a: Only the first site meets all of his conditions at once: fortification, land that sustains people, water not only from rain, and good roads and waterways. Each other site fails one stated condition.

questions.q: A museum caption reads: 'All sixteen mahajanapada capitals were large fortified cities, and none of them is a living city today.' Do you agree? Check each half against the chapter and correct it.
questions.a: No: both halves overstate. The chapter says most capitals were fairly large, well-fortified cities with a moat (not all), and that most of those ancient capitals continue to be living cities today, often 2,500 years old (not none). Corrected: 'Most mahajanapada capitals were large fortified cities, and most are living cities today.'
s: Verdict: disagrees, both halves overstate
First half: 'most' were large, well-fortified cities, not all
Second half: most continue to be living cities, often 2,500 years old

questions.q: A guide at a ruin says, 'The words sabha and samiti were first used by the Vajji gana when it began to vote.' Which comment fits the chapter?
o: The words first appear in the Vedas, and every janapada already had such an assembly
The words first appear in the Buddhist texts, long after the Vajji gana had come to an end
The words were coined for ganas alone, since a monarchy had no assembly of any kind
The words came from Magadha, whose raja was the first to call an assembly of elders
questions.a: The book says every janapada had a sabha or samiti and reminds us that the words first appear in the Vedas, India's most ancient texts, so they are far older than the Vajji gana and were not special to ganas.

questions.q: In a state, a council debated whether to raise a new army. Members voted when they disagreed, and the same council then chose who should be ruler. How would the book describe this state?
o: A gana or sangha, an early republic
A monarchy like Magadha, since every state had a raja
A janapada, since only smaller states had assemblies
A mahajanapada with no assembly at all
questions.a: Monarchies had hereditary rulers, and the council that voted and chose the ruler marks a gana. The 'janapada with only small states having assemblies' idea is wrong since every janapada had an assembly.

questions.q: True or False: 'A rājā of Magadha who always took advice from an assembly of elders and his ministers could still be called the ultimate authority of his state.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. In a monarchy the raja was the ultimate authority, supported by ministers and an assembly of elders; taking advice did not remove his final say, and his position remained hereditary.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: in a monarchy the raja is supported and advised by ministers and an assembly but remains the ultimate authority

questions.q:
A student's project says: 'In ancient India an assembly could remove any ruler.' Her teacher asks her to check every word against the chapter before the project is displayed.
(a) Which word in the sentence goes beyond the chapter, and which phrase does the chapter use to show that the claim comes only from some sources?
(b) The chapter calls such mentions significant, yet adds a caution. State the caution and the reason it gives.
(c) A second student offers: 'According to some texts an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler, so assemblies controlled every raja.' Which part still goes too far?
(d) Write a version that keeps the project's point but stays true to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 'Any': the chapter says an incompetent ruler; the phrase 'according to some texts' marks the limited source. (b) It does not mean this was an established law, because the data we have for such remote periods is incomplete. (c) 'Assemblies controlled every raja': the chapter says a good ruler was supposed to take advice from assemblies, while in a monarchy the raja was the ultimate authority. (d) For example: 'According to some texts, an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler, though this may not have been an established law.'
s: Part (a): 'any' overreaches; 'according to some texts' is the chapter's hedge
Part (b): not an established law, because data for remote periods is incomplete
Part (c): 'controlled every raja' overreaches: the raja was the ultimate authority in a monarchy and was only expected to take advice
Part (d): a version that keeps 'some texts', 'incompetent' and a caution

questions.q:
Match each line of an invented record in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. Each ruler in the list is the son of the one before  2. The council debated a war and settled it by a vote  3. The council chose a successor when the head died  4. The ruler heard his elders and then gave the final order himself
Column II: a. Monarchy, because succession followed birth  b. Gana, because the assembly took the major decisions  c. Gana, because the assembly selected the ruler  d. Monarchy, because the raja was the ultimate authority
questions.a: Succession by birth and the ruler's final order mark a monarchy; settling a war by vote is the assembly taking a major decision, and choosing the successor is the assembly selecting the ruler, which mark a gana. Swapping the two gana features, or the two monarchy features, is the usual slip.

questions.q: The chapter says of the assembly of a janapada, 'We may assume that most of the members were elders in the clan.' (a) What does the phrase 'We may assume' tell us about this statement? (b) A student concludes, 'So no young person could ever sit in the sabha.' Judge her conclusion.
questions.a: (a) It is a reasoned guess, not something the sources record. (b) It goes too far: the chapter says 'most' of the members, not all, and says it only as an assumption.
s: Part (a): 'may assume' marks an assumption, not a recorded fact
Part (b): 'most' is not 'all' and the statement is only an assumption, so the conclusion overreaches

questions.q:
A historian reads sources on two invented states. Rampur: the ruler is the son of the last ruler; the elders meet and are consulted; the ruler gives the final order on taxes and war. Sundarnagar: an assembly meets, debates and votes when members disagree, and it chose the head of state after each of the last three deaths.
(a) Classify each state as a monarchy or a gana and give the one fact on which each classification rests.
(b) A student argues that both states are ganas because both have an assembly. Use the chapter to answer her.
(c) The sources for Sundarnagar cover only three reigns. Using the chapter's caution about remote periods, say how far the historian may generalise.
(d) A museum label must say whether Sundarnagar may be called an 'early republic'. Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Rampur is a monarchy, because its ruler is hereditary and gives the final order; Sundarnagar is a gana, because its assembly decides by vote and selects the head. (b) Every janapada had an assembly; what marks a gana is that the assembly takes the major decisions and selects the ruler, which Rampur's elders do not. (c) The chapter says the data for such remote periods is incomplete, so three reigns allow a cautious statement about these reigns, not a general law for the state. (d) Yes, with a hedge: the chapter's criterion for early republics (the assembly decides and selects the ruler) is met, so the label 'early republic, on the evidence of three reigns' is justified.
s: Part (a): Rampur monarchy (hereditary, final order); Sundarnagar gana (assembly votes and selects the head)
Part (b): every janapada had an assembly; a gana is marked by the assembly deciding and selecting the ruler
Part (c): data for remote periods is incomplete, so generalise only cautiously from three reigns
Part (d): yes, because the criterion is met, with a hedge about the limited evidence

questions.q: Show that one mahajanapada cannot be both a hereditary monarchy with the raja as ultimate authority and a gana in which the assembly selects the ruler.
questions.a: In a monarchy the position is hereditary and the raja is the last word; in a gana the assembly chooses the ruler and decides major matters. The source of authority differs, so a state is one or the other.
s: Monarchy: raja is the son of the previous one and the final authority
Gana: the assembly selects the ruler and decides by vote
These put the final say in different places, so a state cannot be both at once

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Magadha, Kosala and Avanti the position of raja was hereditary.
Reason (R): The raja collected taxes, maintained law and order and kept an army.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: Both true, but the raja's duties do not explain why the position was passed from father to son.

questions.q: In a state, the ruler is the son of the last ruler. He hears the elders and his ministers on a plan to build a new rampart, and then orders it himself. Which description fits best?
o: A monarchy, with the raja the ultimate authority
A gana, because an assembly of elders was present
An early republic, because members were consulted before the decision
A janapada without any assembly, because one person decided
questions.a: Every janapada had an assembly; consulting it does not make a state a gana. In a gana the assembly decides and selects the ruler.

questions.q: A chronicle line reads: 'When the head died, the council met under the great tree, spoke for three days, and then voted; Dhruv received 22 of the 30 votes and was named head.' (a) Give two features of this line that mark a gana and not a monarchy. (b) What percentage of the votes did Dhruv receive? Give it to one decimal place.
questions.a: (a) The assembly took the decision by discussion followed by a vote, and it selected the head instead of the position passing from father to son. (b) 22/30 = 73.3 percent.
s: Part (a): discussion then vote, and the assembly selected the head (not hereditary)
Part (b): 73.3 percent

questions.q: A record of the invented state Veerapur says: (1) the ruler consults the elders' council before changing a tax; (2) on the ruler's death his eldest son takes the throne; (3) the council votes on whether to go to war; (4) the ruler keeps an army and has a rampart built round the capital; (5) a local text says the council could remove an incompetent ruler. Sort the five features by what they point to, say which feature the chapter treats as a mere possibility, and decide with reasons whether Veerapur is a monarchy or a gana.
questions.a: (1) and (4) fit a monarchy: the raja is advised by an assembly and keeps the army and fortifications. (2) is hereditary succession: monarchy. (3) the assembly deciding by vote points towards a gana. (5) is like the chapter's 'according to some texts' removal, which does not show an established law, so it proves nothing. Decision: Veerapur is best called a monarchy, since the chapter's marker of a gana is the assembly selecting the ruler and here the ruler is hereditary; (3) shows an unusually strong council but does not change that.
s: (1) and (4) point to a monarchy (advice from an assembly; army and fortifications)
(2) hereditary succession points to a monarchy
(3) a vote on war points towards a gana
(5) is a text's claim, like 'according to some texts', not an established law
Decision: monarchy, because the ruler is hereditary and not selected by the assembly

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Vajji and Malla are called early republics.
Reason (R): In Vajji and Malla the assembly selected the ruler, which makes them the earliest republic in the world.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: A is true. R overclaims and is false: the chapter says these are 'one of the earliest such systems in the world', not the earliest; the selection of the ruler by the assembly is true but the conclusion drawn from it is not.

questions.q: A student writes, 'Vajji and Malla were the only two mahajanapadas in which the assembly selected the raja.' Which comment fits the chapter's wording?
o: It says 'at least two', so others may have shared the system; it names only these two
The claim is exactly right, since the chapter states that there were two such states and no more
The claim is wrong, since the chapter names Magadha as a third state of the same kind
The claim is exactly right, since monarchies could never have an assembly with any power
questions.a: The book says 'at least two mahajanapadas, Vajji and the neighbouring Malla, had a different system', so more may have existed and 'only two' goes beyond the text. Magadha is a monarchy, and monarchies had an advisory assembly.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: In some mahajanapadas the assembly decided important matters through discussion and, if necessary, through vote.
Statement 2: The texts prove that an incompetent ruler was always removed by the assembly in every state.
Statement 3: A good ruler was not expected to rule arbitrarily but to take advice from assemblies, ministers and administrators.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: only some texts mention removal, and the book cautions that this was not an established law.

questions.q: Describe an imaginary state in which an assembly of elders exists and yet the state is a monarchy, not a gana. Say what the assembly does and what it does not do.
questions.a: Example: In Kosalpur the elders meet and advise the raja on taxes, but the raja is the late raja's son and takes the final decision; the assembly neither chooses him nor decides by vote, so it is a monarchy.
s: Assembly exists and is consulted
Raja is hereditary and the ultimate authority
Assembly advises but does not select the ruler or decide by vote

questions.q: A museum must pick one title for a wall on governance in the mahajanapadas. Title 1: 'Early India was ruled only by kings'. Title 2: 'Early India had kings advised by assemblies, and also states run through their assemblies'. Title 3: 'Early India was made up only of republics'. Choose the title that fits the chapter and justify it with four points from the chapter, rejecting the other two.
questions.a: Title 2. Every janapada had a sabha or samiti and a good ruler was supposed to take advice from it. In monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti the raja was the ultimate authority, supported by ministers and an assembly of elders. In Vajji and Malla the assembly took major decisions by discussion and vote and selected the ruler. Title 1 ignores the ganas and the role of assemblies; Title 3 ignores the monarchies.
s: Chooses Title 2
Every janapada had an assembly and a good ruler took its advice
Monarchies (Magadha, Kosala, Avanti): hereditary raja as ultimate authority
Ganas (Vajji, Malla): the assembly decided by vote and selected the ruler
Rejects Title 1 (ignores ganas and assemblies) and Title 3 (ignores monarchies)

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Vajji was a gana because it had an assembly, whereas Magadha had none.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly. He is right that Vajji was a gana, but wrong about Magadha: as a monarchy it was supported by ministers and an assembly of elders. What makes Vajji a gana is that its assembly took the major decisions and even selected the ruler.
s: Verdict: partly right
The wrong part: Magadha, a monarchy, also had an assembly of elders
The right marker: in Vajji the assembly took major decisions and selected the ruler

questions.q: A trader says, 'In Vajji any person of the town could vote on the choice of raja.' (a) Whom does the chapter name as the ones who selected the ruler? (b) The chapter says the functioning of the ganas 'might be called' democratic. What does the word 'might' warn us about the trader's claim?
questions.a: (a) The members of the assembly (the sabha or samiti). (b) That 'democratic' is a description with limits, not a statement that everyone voted; the chapter speaks only of members of the assembly.
s: Part (a): the members of the assembly
Part (b): 'might' signals a cautious label; the chapter does not say that every person voted

questions.q: A ruler ignores his assembly's advice on one matter and nothing happens to him. (a) Does this show the book is wrong to say a good ruler was supposed to take the assembly's advice? Explain. (b) Whom else was a good ruler supposed to take advice from?
questions.a: (a) No. 'Supposed to' states what was expected of a good ruler, not a law; the book itself cautions that the mentions of removal do not mean an established law, and one ruler's lapse does not alter the expectation. (b) Ministers and administrators.
s: Part (a): the book describes an expectation of a good ruler, not an enforced law, so one lapse does not refute it
Part (b): ministers and administrators

questions.q: The chapter says a raja's position was hereditary 'in the sense that a rājā would usually be the son of the previous one'. A raja dies childless and his nephew is crowned. (a) Which word in the chapter leaves room for this? (b) Does the nephew's succession turn the state into a gana? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 'Usually'. (b) No: the position is still passed on within the family and not selected by an assembly, so the state remains a monarchy.
s: Part (a): 'usually'
Part (b): no, succession within the family without the assembly's selection keeps it a monarchy

questions.q: A relief on the Sanchi stupa shows a smithy: several workers bring firewood and water, one stokes the fire and one beats a piece of iron. (a) What does the scene show about how iron objects were made? (b) The chapter says iron tools became part of daily life. How far does this one panel support that statement?
questions.a: (a) Making an iron object needed several workers, each with a task (fuel, water, fire, hammering), so it was a team craft. (b) It fits the statement, since iron-working is shown as an ordinary workshop scene, but one panel is only a sample and cannot show how widespread iron tools were; the chapter's own statement rests on a wider body of evidence.
s: Part (a): several workers, each with a separate task, so iron-working was a team craft
Part (b): it fits but one panel cannot prove how widespread iron tools were

questions.q: A village headman in the late 2nd millennium BCE hears that iron techniques were perfected long ago, and wants iron ploughshares for all his farmers at once. (a) What does the chapter say iron tools facilitated? (b) What does the chapter say about how long it took for iron to become part of daily life after its techniques were perfected, and what should that make him expect?
questions.a: (a) Agriculture on a bigger scale. (b) It took a few centuries after the techniques were perfected, so he should expect the change to be gradual, not immediate; by the late 2nd millennium BCE iron tools had become widespread.
s: Part (a): iron tools facilitated agriculture on a bigger scale
Part (b): a few centuries, so a gradual change is to be expected

questions.q: A new teaching begins in a small town of the Ganga plains in the 1st millennium BCE. Which of these would the chapter name as ways it travelled to other parts of India?
o: Scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India, and people on pilgrimage
Punch-marked silver coins carrying the teaching's symbols from state to state
Iron weapons carried by armies, which forced neighbouring states to accept it
Governors sent out by one empire that already ruled the whole Subcontinent
questions.a: The book says the schools of thought spread their teachings and literature through scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India and people undertaking pilgrimages. It does not say coins carried teachings, that armies forced them, or that a single empire ruled yet.

questions.q: Write a three-line account of a trader in a mahajanapada who pays for goods in a new kind of coin. Line 1 must say why such coins had become necessary; line 2 must say what the first coins were made of and how they were marked; line 3 must say where else he might be able to spend them.
questions.a: Line 1: trade had grown, which made coins necessary. Line 2: the first Indian coins were of silver, a soft metal, with symbols punched into them (punch-marked coins). Line 3: in neighbouring regions too, since coins were exchanged across regions and neighbours' coins were used (even with other parts of the world).
s: Line 1: growing trade made coins necessary
Line 2: silver, a soft metal, with symbols punched in
Line 3: coins were exchanged across regions and neighbours' coins were used

questions.q: A quiz says, 'Iron techniques were perfected in the late 2nd millennium BCE.' Which correction fits the chapter?
o: Techniques were perfected from the early 2nd millennium BCE; tools were widespread by the late 2nd
Techniques were perfected in the 1st millennium BCE, once coins had made trade grow in the Ganga plains
Tools were widespread from the early 2nd millennium BCE, and the techniques were perfected only by the late 2nd
Techniques were perfected in the late 2nd millennium BCE, and the tools became widespread a few centuries before
questions.a: The chapter separates two stages: techniques were perfected in several regions from the early 2nd millennium BCE, and it took a few centuries for iron to enter daily life, so iron tools were widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE. The quiz mixes up the stages.

questions.q: A hoard has 18 silver punch-marked pieces and 6 copper pieces. Since the chapter says the first Indian coins were of one metal and copper coins were made later, at most ___ of the 24 pieces could belong to the very first coinage.

Assertion (A): A mahajanapada's coins could turn up in the markets of a neighbouring region.
Reason (R): Coins from neighbouring regions were used and exchanged in trade, though a mahajanapada generally issued its own.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because neighbours' coins were used and exchanged, one state's coins could reach the next region's markets.

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'Iron swords, made by the smiths of the Harappan civilisation.' (a) Using the chapter, give two reasons the label is wrong. (b) Write a corrected label naming the metals the Harappans had mastered.
questions.a: (a) The Harappans mastered copper and bronze metallurgy, while iron metallurgy was the major shift of the Second Urbanisation; and iron tools became widespread only by the late 2nd millennium BCE, long after the Harappan urban order had disintegrated. (b) 'Copper and bronze tools of the Harappan civilisation.'
s: Part (a): the Harappans mastered copper and bronze; iron belongs to the Second Urbanisation and became widespread only by the late 2nd millennium BCE
Part (b): a corrected label naming copper and bronze

questions.q: A school poster says: 'Iron tools helped farming. Iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze. So the mahajanapadas fought constantly.' Which sentence is not supported by the chapter, and why?
questions.a: The last sentence. The first two are in the book, but there is only some evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas and how frequent or intense it was is impossible to tell.
s: Identifies the last sentence as unsupported
Reason: there is only some evidence of warfare
Reason: how frequent or intense it was is impossible to tell

questions.q: Over ten years the traders of Town P come to deal with nine regions, while those of Town Q still deal only with two neighbours. Following the chapter's reasoning about what made coins necessary, which comment is best?
o: P needs coins more as its trade grows, and neighbours' coins will circulate there
Q needs coins more, since fewer trading partners means each deal must be settled in coin
Neither needs coins, since the first coins were meant for use inside one state only
Both need coins equally, since each state generally issued its own coins
questions.a: The book says the first use of coins was made necessary by growing trade, and that coins from neighbouring regions were used as well as exchanged. P's trade has grown, so the need is greater there.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Because iron weapons were better than bronze ones, the chapter concludes that the mahajanapadas fought each other constantly.
Reason (R): The chapter says it is impossible to tell how frequent or how intense the warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas was.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says iron made lighter, sharper weapons and that there is some evidence of warfare, but it draws no conclusion about constant fighting. R is true and is the very reason A fails.

questions.q: A student writes, 'Wars between the mahajanapadas were the only thing that gave rise to new kingdoms and empires.' (a) Which words in the chapter's sentence correct her? (b) The same student adds, 'so wars must have been very frequent.' Why does the chapter not allow this?
questions.a: (a) The chapter says 'such military campaigns, but occasionally alliances too', gave rise to new kingdoms and empires. (b) It says there is some evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas but how frequent or intense it was is impossible to tell.
s: Part (a): campaigns, but occasionally alliances too
Part (b): frequency and intensity of warfare are impossible to tell

questions.q:
A museum catalogue lists 40 finds from one region: 14 copper or bronze tools, 12 iron tools, 8 silver punch-marked coins and 6 copper coins. The curator has one case with room for exactly 20 objects, titled 'What was new in the age of the mahajanapadas'.
(a) Which finds does the chapter clearly tie to the Second Urbanisation, and how many are there in all?
(b) The 14 copper or bronze tools do not suit the case's theme. Why not, using the chapter?
(c) What percentage of the coins are silver (one decimal place), and which coin group does the chapter say came first?
(d) Choose the 20 objects for the case and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Iron tools, silver coins and copper coins: 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 finds. (b) The Harappans had already mastered copper and bronze, so those metals were not new in this age. (c) 8/14 = 57.1 percent; the chapter says the first coins were silver and copper coins came later. (d) The 12 iron tools and the 8 silver coins: both are new in this age and the silver coins are the first coins, whereas the copper coins are later issues.
s: Part (a): iron tools, silver coins and copper coins, 26 in all
Part (b): the Harappans had already mastered copper and bronze, so they are not new
Part (c): 57.1 percent; silver coins came first
Part (d): 12 iron tools and 8 silver coins, justified as what was new and earliest

questions.q: A classmate says, 'In the age of the mahajanapadas, iron changed life more than coins did.' Take a side and argue it using the chapter, giving two points for your side, one point for the other side, and one limit on what the chapter can tell us.
questions.a: Either side may be argued with chapter points. For iron: it facilitated agriculture on a bigger scale and made lighter, sharper weapons than bronze. For coins: growing trade made them necessary, and they were exchanged across regions and even with other parts of the world. A limit: the chapter says how frequent or intense warfare was is impossible to tell, so the effect of iron weapons cannot be measured; it also gives no figures to compare the two innovations. Full marks need two points for the side chosen, one for the other side and the limit.
s: States a side clearly
Two chapter points for the chosen side
One chapter point for the other side
Names one limit of the evidence (warfare frequency impossible to tell, or no figures to compare)
The conclusion follows from the points given

questions.q: A display case shows five punch-marked silver coins from five different cities of north India, each bearing different symbols. (a) What does the variety of symbols suggest about who issued the coins, according to the chapter? (b) A coin of city A is found in the ruins of city B, which lies in a neighbouring region. What does the chapter let us conclude?
questions.a: (a) Generally a mahajanapada issued its own coins, so different states' coins carried different symbols. (b) That coins from neighbouring regions were used as well as exchanged in trade; the find does not show that city B was ruled from city A.
s: Part (a): each mahajanapada generally issued its own coins
Part (b): neighbouring regions' coins were used and exchanged in trade

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Iron techniques were perfected in several regions from the early 2nd millennium BCE, but iron tools were widespread only by the late 2nd millennium BCE.
Statement 2: The first Indian coins were of silver, and each mahajanapada used only its own coins.
Statement 3: The presence of iron weapons shows that the mahajanapadas fought many wars.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is as the chapter says. Statement 2 fails on 'only': neighbours' coins were used as well. Statement 3 is not shown: how frequent warfare was is impossible to tell.

questions.q: A classmate's notebook says: 'The moment iron techniques were perfected in the early 2nd millennium BCE, everyone in India was using iron tools.' Use the chapter to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says perfecting iron techniques and using iron every day were different; it took a few centuries, and iron tools were widespread only by the late 2nd millennium BCE.
s: States that techniques were perfected from the early 2nd millennium BCE
States that it took a few centuries for iron to become part of daily life
Notes that iron tools became widespread only by the late 2nd millennium BCE

questions.q: True or False: 'The chapter says iron made lighter and sharper weapons than bronze, yet it does not allow us to say how often the mahajanapadas fought.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. Better weapons are one thing; the chapter says there is only some evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas, and how frequent or intense it was is impossible to tell.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: only some evidence of warfare exists and its frequency and intensity cannot be told

questions.q: A student writes a chain: 'Trade grew, so coins became necessary; coins were exchanged across regions; coins were used to pay for iron, so iron tools spread.' Which link goes beyond what the chapter says?
o: Coins were used to pay for iron, so iron tools spread
Trade grew, so coins became necessary
Coins were exchanged across different regions
Iron tools had become widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE
questions.a: The chapter says growing trade made coins necessary and that coins were exchanged across regions; it also says iron tools became widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE. It never says coins paid for iron or that this spread iron.

questions.q: A site shows three layers. Layer X: copper and bronze tools only. Layer Y: 4 copper tools, 6 iron tools and 2 silver punch-marked coins. Layer Z: 15 iron tools, 9 silver coins and 5 copper coins. (a) Put the layers in the order the chapter's account suggests, earliest first, and give one reason. (b) What does the rise in iron tools from Y to Z fit in the chapter? (c) Which layer holds the earliest coins at the site?
questions.a: (a) X, Y, Z: only X lacks both iron and coins, and copper coins appear only in Z, whereas the first coins were silver and copper ones came later. (b) Iron taking a few centuries to become part of daily life and becoming widespread. (c) Layer Y, which holds only silver coins.
s: Part (a): X, Y, Z with a reason (no iron or coins in X; copper coins only in Z)
Part (b): iron gradually becoming part of daily life and widespread
Part (c): Layer Y, with only silver coins

questions.q:
A student's answer paragraph has four sentences. S1: 'Coins were first used in India in the age of the mahajanapadas.' S2: 'The first coins were made of gold, a soft metal.' S3: 'Every state used only its own coins.' S4: 'Iron techniques were perfected in the late 2nd millennium BCE, so iron weapons ended warfare.'
(a) Which sentence is correct as it stands?
(b) Correct S2 and S3 using the chapter.
(c) S4 has two errors. Name both.
(d) Rewrite S4 in one sentence that is true to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) S1. (b) S2: the first coins were silver, a soft metal, with copper, gold and others later. S3: a state generally issued its own coins, but coins from neighbouring regions were used and exchanged as well. (c) The date (techniques were perfected from the early 2nd millennium BCE; the tools were widespread by the late 2nd), and the claim that better weapons ended warfare (the chapter says there is some evidence of warfare, frequency impossible to tell). (d) For example: 'Iron techniques were perfected from the early 2nd millennium BCE, and iron made lighter, sharper weapons than bronze.'
s: Part (a): S1
Part (b): S2 silver (gold later); S3 neighbours' coins were also used
Part (c): the date, and the claim that warfare ended
Part (d): a true rewrite with the correct date and no claim about ending warfare

questions.q: Around 600 BCE a trader and a Buddhist nun leave a Ganga-plains city for a city three regions away. The trader carries an iron tool and a silver punch-marked coin; the nun carries a text. For each of the three objects, say whether the chapter supports its reaching the distant city and give the chapter's support, and then name one thing the chapter cannot tell us about the journey.
questions.a: Text: supported, because schools of thought spread their teachings and literature through monks, nuns and scholars travelling across India. Iron tool: supported, since iron tools had become widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE, well before 600 BCE. Coin: supported, since coins were exchanged across different regions and neighbours' coins were used; a city three regions away is more than a neighbour, so acceptance there is not shown by the chapter. The chapter cannot tell us how the journey went, for instance how accepted the coin would be so far away.
s: Text: supported through travelling monks, nuns and scholars
Iron tool: supported since iron tools were widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE
Coin: supported since coins were exchanged across regions
Notes that neighbours' coins are what the chapter mentions, so acceptance three regions away is less certain
Names a limit: the chapter does not describe this journey or the coin's reception

questions.q: A student says, 'The English word caste is as old as the Vedas, which is why it names the Vedic four-fold scheme.' Which comment fits the chapter?
o: It comes from the Portuguese casta of 16th-century travellers; scholars use it for varnas, jatis or the system
It comes from the Vedic texts, but scholars apply it only to jatis, the communities each tied to one occupation
It was coined by Vedic scholars for the four varnas, and the Portuguese later borrowed it for the many jatis
It comes from a Portuguese word, and scholars apply it only to the four varnas described in the Vedic texts
questions.a: The book says 'caste' comes from the Portuguese word casta, as Portuguese travellers of the 16th century CE tried to make sense of Indian society; a few scholars apply it to varnas, most to jatis, and others to the whole varna-jati system. The Vedic concept is varna, not caste.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A sub-jati is a group formed when several jatis join together and share one set of customs.
Statement 2: Varna is a concept that emerged from the Vedic texts and has five groups.
Statement 3: Scholars differ on whether 'caste' refers to varnas, to jatis or to the whole varna-jati system.
Which statements are correct?
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: a sub-jati is a subdivision of a jati with customs of its own. Statement 2 is false: there are four varnas. Statement 3 is as the chapter says.

questions.q: A historian finds one old text that tells of a family of farmers who left their village after a long drought and became craftspeople in a city. How far does the chapter let her use it?
o: As one case of a pattern the chapter backs with texts and inscriptions, though one text is only one case
As proof that no family of farmers could ever remain farmers, since the text shows the opposite of stability
As proof that the system was already rigid, since the family needed a drought to change its work
As a record of a new varna, since craftspeople are a different group from farmers
questions.a: The book says there is historical evidence in texts and inscriptions that individuals and communities changed occupations if circumstances demanded, and gives a drought as an example. One text is a case of that pattern, not proof of a general rule, and it does not show rigidity or a new varna.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The varna-jati system gave Indian society some stability.
Reason (R): The system structured society and organised its activities, including economic ones.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: Both true; organising society and its activities is why it gave stability.

questions.q: A student says: 'In the early period nobody could change an occupation, so no Brahmin could ever have taken up trade.' Use the chapter to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says there is historical evidence in texts and inscriptions that individuals and communities changed occupations if circumstances demanded, for instance some Brahmins turned to trade or even military activities.
s: States that texts and inscriptions give evidence of changed occupations
Gives the example of some Brahmins turning to trade or military activities
Concludes the early system was more flexible

questions.q: True or False: 'The chapter says the varna-jati system was rigid in the early period and became more flexible with the passage of time.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The system was significantly different, more flexible, in earlier periods and became more rigid with the passage of time; texts and inscriptions show people changing occupations when circumstances demanded.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it was more flexible early and became more rigid later, with evidence of changing occupations in the early period

questions.q: A student concludes: 'Everything about the organisation of ancient Indian society can be explained by the varna-jati system alone.' Which line of the chapter weakens her conclusion?
o: It is an important mechanism at work in society, but not the only one; there have been many others
Scholars disagree on whether 'caste' refers to varnas, to jatis or to the whole varna-jati system
A jati could be divided into sub-jatis, each with customs of its own about marriage, rituals or food
The word 'caste' comes from a Portuguese word used by travellers who visited India in the 16th century
questions.a: The book says varna-jati has been an important mechanism at work in Indian society, but it is not the only one. The other lines are true but say nothing about whether the system is the only explanation.

questions.q: (a) The chapter says that in an ideal society the groups would complement one another, but that most of the time something else follows. What follows? (b) It adds that equality is an ideal 'very few, if any' societies have achieved. A student concludes, 'So no society has ever had any equality.' Judge her conclusion.
questions.a: (a) The divisions lead to inequalities: some groups acquire more wealth, power or influence than others. (b) She goes too far: the chapter says 'very few, if any' have achieved the ideal, which is a hedge and is about fully achieving equality, not about having some.
s: Part (a): divisions often lead to inequalities, with some groups gaining more wealth, power or influence
Part (b): 'very few, if any' is a hedge and is about fully achieving the ideal, so 'no equality at all' overreaches

questions.q: Three historians sum up the varna-jati system. H1: 'It was rigid from the very start.' H2: 'It was always flexible and has never changed.' H3: 'It was more flexible in the early period and became more rigid with time, in particular during British rule.' Judge each one using the chapter and say which the chapter supports, naming the strength of that support.
questions.a: H1 fails: texts and inscriptions show people and communities changing occupations when circumstances demanded, for example farmers moving to a city or some Brahmins taking to trade. H2 fails: in time the system became rigid and led to inequalities and discrimination, in particular during British rule. H3 is supported: the chapter says there is a broad agreement that the system was significantly more flexible in earlier periods and became more rigid with time. 'Broad agreement' is strong but not unanimous support.
s: H1 rejected, with the evidence from texts and inscriptions of changed occupations
An example of changed occupation (drought-hit farmers or Brahmins in trade or military activity)
H2 rejected: the system became rigid, with inequality and discrimination
H3 supported, with 'in particular during British rule'
Names the strength: a broad agreement among scholars, not unanimity

questions.q: Four people: (i) a woman who teaches sacred knowledge and conducts rituals; (ii) a captain who guards the frontier and leads soldiers; (iii) a man who runs a cloth shop and also farms land; (iv) a blacksmith who makes ploughs. Place each in the chapter's four-fold varna scheme.
