Then, the blacksmith's family has made ploughs for six generations, and his cousins, who make the same tools, follow different marriage and food customs: name the term for the family and the term for his cousins' group, and say why 'varna' and the family's own label are not the same kind of label.
questions.a: (i) Brahmin; (ii) Kshatriya; (iii) Vaishya, whose occupations include trade, business or agriculture; (iv) Shudra, as an artisan or craftsperson. The blacksmith's family is a jati, a community with a specific occupation whose skill passes down the generations; his cousins' group is a sub-jati, a division with customs of its own. Varna is a Vedic concept with four broad groups, while jati is an occupational community, so they are labels of different kinds.
s: Places all four people correctly (all four earn 2 marks, two or three earn 1)
Jati for the family
Sub-jati for the cousins' group
Varna is a Vedic four-group concept, jati an occupational community

questions.q: A student writes, 'The chapter says the varna-jati system became rigid only after British rule began.' (a) Which words in the chapter correct the word 'only'? (b) What does the chapter say about the system's rigidity before that period?
questions.a: (a) 'In particular during the British rule' says rigidity grew especially then; it does not say that was the only time. (b) The system became more rigid 'with the passage of time', so rigidity was already growing earlier.
s: Part (a): 'in particular during the British rule' marks emphasis, not exclusivity
Part (b): it became more rigid with the passage of time, not suddenly

questions.q:
A museum in Madurai will show one panel on the early varna-jati system. Its brief is to show what the chapter says was different about the early system when compared with the later one. Panel P: families changed trades when circumstances demanded; farmers became craftspeople and some Brahmins took to trade. Panel Q: each jati kept its own occupation, skills passed from parent to child, and each sub-jati had its own marriage and food customs.
(a) Which panel shows a feature that the chapter says was more marked in the early period?
(b) What kinds of ancient evidence does the chapter cite for that feature?
(c) What does the chapter say the system gave society, and how does it sit alongside Panel P's changes?
(d) Write a one-line caption for the chosen panel that does not claim more than the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Panel P: the chapter says the system was significantly different, more flexible, in earlier periods. (b) Texts and inscriptions. (c) It structured society, organised its activities, including economic ones, and gave it some stability, so the changes of Panel P sat inside an ordered system. (d) For example: 'In the early period, texts and inscriptions show, families could change their occupations when circumstances demanded.' A caption using 'always' or 'anyone' claims too much.
s: Part (a): Panel P, the flexibility of the early period
Part (b): texts and inscriptions
Part (c): organised society and gave some stability, alongside changes of occupation
Part (d): a caption that is true to the chapter and avoids 'always' or 'anyone'

questions.q: A worksheet key says: 'Sub-jati: a division of a jati that develops customs and traditions of its own. Caste: the English word, from the Portuguese casta, which most scholars apply to jatis.' Do you agree with the key? Check each definition against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says a jati often gets subdivided into sub-jatis, each developing customs of its own about marriage, rituals or food habits. It says 'caste' comes from the Portuguese casta and that, although a few scholars apply it to varnas and others to the whole system, most apply it to jatis.
s: Verdict: agrees with the key
Sub-jati checked: a division of a jati with customs of its own
Caste checked: from Portuguese casta, applied by most scholars to jatis

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Because the varna-jati system gave Indian society some stability, it cannot have led to inequalities.
Reason (R): The chapter says that in time the system became rigid and led to inequalities and discrimination towards the lower jatis and some excluded communities.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
questions.a: A is false: stability and inequality can exist together, as the chapter's account of the system shows. R is true and is the very reason A fails.

questions.q: In a 1st-millennium BCE town, the group of metal-workers gains more wealth and influence than the group of porters, and the porters' children find it hard to leave porters' work. Which statement matches the chapter's account?
o: Group divisions often lead to inequalities, and the system grew more rigid in time
Such a gap shows the system was rigid from its very beginning, in every earlier period too
Such a gap shows that porters formed a separate varna with a Vedic origin in the sacred texts
Such a gap is the stability the system gave, so it needs no further explanation at all
questions.a: The chapter says that most of the time divisions lead to inequalities, with some groups acquiring more wealth, power or influence, and that the system became more rigid with the passage of time. It does not say it was rigid from the start, that porters were a separate varna, or that inequality is the stability it gave.

questions.q: Describe one everyday situation of your own, not from the book, that shows a jati, and explain what makes it a jati and not a varna.
questions.a: Example: a family of bell-metal workers in a town whose skill passes from parent to child. It is a jati because it is a community with a specific occupation tied to livelihood; a varna is one of four broad groups from Vedic texts.
s: Gives a believable situation of a group tied to an occupation
Shows skills passed from generation to generation
Explains that a jati is an occupational community, whereas varna is one of four Vedic groups

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the term in Column II.
Column I: 1. A family of stone-masons whose skill passes from parent to child for generations  2. A group of that family's descendants who keep their own food customs  3. All who are expected to defend the land and fight if necessary  4. The English word, from a Portuguese word, that most scholars apply to jatis
Column II: a. Kshatriyas  b. Sub-jati  c. Jati  d. Caste
questions.a: The masons' family is a jati; the descendants with their own customs are a sub-jati; those expected to defend the land are the Kshatriyas; and 'caste' is the English word from the Portuguese casta. Swapping jati and sub-jati is the usual slip.

questions.q: A student's essay says, 'The British created the varna-jati system.' Which sentence from a corrected essay stays within the chapter?
o: Scholars broadly agree the system was more flexible early and grew more rigid, in particular under British rule
The chapter proves that the system was rigid before British rule began and became flexible once that rule started
The chapter shows that the system began with British rule and had no earlier existence in India
The chapter says the system was equally rigid in every period and changed only in its names
questions.a: The chapter says the varna concept emerged from the Vedic texts and jatis were occupational communities long before; the broad agreement is that the system was more flexible in earlier periods and became more rigid with the passage of time, in particular during British rule.

questions.q:
A museum exhibit on the varna-jati system uses invented records. Section 1 (1st millennium BCE): 5 records, 4 of which show a family or community changing its occupation when circumstances demanded. Section 2 (British rule): 6 records, 5 of which show children bound to their parents' occupation with no change possible.
(a) Work out the percentage of records showing the stated pattern in each section, to one decimal place.
(b) Which statement of the chapter do the two percentages, taken together, support?
(c) The chapter names one benefit and one problem of the system. State both.
(d) The curator must choose a title: 'A system that never changed' or 'A system that grew more rigid'. Decide and justify using (a) to (c), noting one limit of the records.
questions.a: (a) 4/5 = 80.0 percent; 5/6 = 83.3 percent. (b) That the system was significantly more flexible in earlier periods and became more rigid with time, in particular during British rule. (c) Benefit: it organised society and its activities and gave it some stability; problem: it became rigid and led to inequalities and discrimination. (d) 'A system that grew more rigid': the flexible records come from the early section and the bound records from the later one. One limit is that the sections hold only 5 and 6 records, so they are a small sample.
s: Part (a): 80.0 percent and 83.3 percent
Part (b): more flexible earlier, more rigid later, in particular under British rule
Part (c): stability as the benefit; rigidity, inequality and discrimination as the problem
Part (d): chooses 'grew more rigid' with a reason and names the small sample as a limit

questions.q: The chapter says Kshatriyas 'were expected to defend the society and the land, and to engage in warfare if necessary'. A student writes, 'So only Kshatriyas ever took part in military activity.' (a) Which words in the chapter's sentence show a role, not an exclusive right? (b) What does the chapter say about some Brahmins that also contradicts the student?
questions.a: (a) 'Were expected to' and 'if necessary' describe a role, not a monopoly. (b) Some Brahmins would turn to trade or even military activities when circumstances demanded.
s: Part (a): 'were expected to' and 'if necessary' show a role, not an exclusive right
Part (b): some Brahmins turned to trade or even military activities

questions.q: (a) In a school play the characters are a priest who performs rituals, a commander in battle, a grain merchant and a craftsperson. Name the varna each belongs to in the chapter's scheme. (b) The play shows the merchant's family also farming. Does this go against the chapter? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra. (b) No. The chapter says Vaishyas were supposed to increase the society's wealth through occupations of trade, business or agriculture.
s: Part (a): Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra in order
Part (b): agriculture is among the Vaishya occupations, so farming does not contradict the chapter

questions.q: A historian notes that a community lived in a town of the period yet stood outside the varna-jati scheme. What does the chapter say about communities in that position?
o: As the system became rigid, discrimination fell on lower jatis and on some communities excluded from it
They formed a fifth varna that the Vedic texts added to the four Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras
They were the Shudras, since the chapter says Shudras were the groups left out of the system altogether
They never existed, since the chapter says every community belonged to a jati and to a varna
questions.a: The chapter says that in time the system became rigid and led to inequalities and discrimination towards the lower jatis or some communities excluded from the varna-jati system. It names four varnas only, and Shudras were artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants within the scheme.

questions.q: A teacher says, 'The cities of the far south appeared only after the mahajanapadas of the north had vanished.' Which comment fits the chapter's dates?
o: No: southern cities began from about 400 BCE, while the mahajanapadas ceased only by 300 or 200 BCE
Yes: the chapter says southern cities began from about 300 BCE, once the mahajanapadas had ceased
No: the chapter says southern cities began about 1900 BCE, long before any mahajanapada existed
Yes: the chapter says the cities of the south were founded by the surviving mahajanapadas of the north
questions.a: The book says southern cities began emerging from about 400 BCE and that the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by 300 or 200 BCE, so the two overlapped for roughly a century or more. The other options invent dates or a founding by the northern states.

questions.q: Sisupalgarh, the capital of the Kalinga region, today lies in a suburb of Bhubaneswar and was first excavated in 1948. (a) A student says a place that is now a suburb cannot have been an ancient capital. Give one reason from the chapter why she is wrong. (b) What does the year 1948 tell us about how we know its plan and fortifications?
questions.a: (a) The chapter says most ancient capitals continue to be living cities today, often 2,500 years old, and it names Sisupalgarh as now part of Bhubaneswar. (b) Its plan and fortifications became known through excavation, which began in 1948.
s: Part (a): ancient capitals often continue as living cities, and Sisupalgarh is now part of Bhubaneswar
Part (b): excavation, first done in 1948, revealed the plan and fortifications

questions.q: Write three lines of directions for a trader going from Takshashila in the northwest to eastern India and then to a port. Line 1 must name the route and what it connects; line 2 the kind of road he takes to the port; line 3 what he finds at the port.
questions.a: Line 1: the Uttarapatha, which connected the northwest regions to the Ganga plains and all the way to eastern India. Line 2: a lateral road, which connected other parts of India with the important ports of the eastern coast. Line 3: a vibrant centre of trade.
s: Line 1: the Uttarapatha from the northwest through the Ganga plains to eastern India
Line 2: a lateral road to a port on the eastern coast
Line 3: a vibrant centre of trade

questions.q: The chapter says the southern regions profitably traded because of what they were rich in. (a) Name two such resources. (b) A student adds, 'and the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas themselves carried these goods to Central Asia.' Which part of her sentence does the chapter not support?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: precious and semiprecious stones, gold, spices. (b) The chapter says the south traded with the rest of India and with kingdoms and empires overseas; it does not say that the three kingdoms carried goods to Central Asia.
s: Part (a): two of stones, gold, spices
Part (b): the carrying of goods to Central Asia by the three kingdoms is not in the chapter

questions.q: A student writes, 'By 300 BCE every region of the Subcontinent was connected, and goods and culture always reached Central and Southeast Asia.' (a) Which word in the chapter's sentence about the Subcontinent corrects 'every'? (b) Which word in its sentence about regions beyond India corrects 'always'?
questions.a: (a) 'Almost': almost the entire Subcontinent, including regions in the Northeast, was one interconnected land. (b) 'Often': goods and culture often travelled beyond India to parts of Central and Southeast Asia.
s: Part (a): 'almost the entire Subcontinent'
Part (b): 'often' beyond India

questions.q: True or False: 'Because the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi, the chapter treats it as the route linking the northwest regions to the Ganga plains and eastern India.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. That is the Uttarapatha. The chapter says the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi and crossed the Vindhya Range of hills to proceed all the way south.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the route linking the northwest to the Ganga plains and eastern India is the Uttarapatha; the Dakshinapatha goes south from Kaushambi across the Vindhyas

questions.q:
Assertion (A): By 300 or 200 BCE almost the entire Subcontinent was one vibrant interconnected land.
Reason (R): The mahajanapadas ceased to exist about the same time.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: Both true, but the end of the mahajanapadas is not the reason regions were connected; roads, ports and trade are.

questions.q: The chapter says southern cities began emerging from about 400 BCE, although recent excavations claim signs of commercial activity going further back. Which find would count as evidence for the recent claim?
o: A dated layer at a southern site, older than 400 BCE, holding traces of trade goods such as beads
A Tamil poem of about 300 BCE that names the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas and several of their kings
A lateral road linking a southern town to a western port, built about 400 BCE, with a busy harbour
A fortified eastern city with a strict square plan and broad streets, dated to about 400 BCE too
questions.a: The claim is about commercial activity in the south older than 400 BCE, so only a dated southern layer older than 400 BCE with trade goods would support it. A later poem, a road built about 400 BCE, or an eastern city do not.

questions.q: The chapter says that southern cities began emerging from about 400 BCE and that 'around this time' the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas emerged. A student concludes, 'So the three kingdoms had already existed for centuries before the cities began.' (a) Which words in the chapter correct her? (b) What does the chapter name as two kinds of evidence for those kingdoms?
questions.a: (a) 'Around this time' places the kingdoms' emergence at about the same time as the cities, not centuries earlier. (b) Archaeological evidence and the most ancient Tamil literature.
s: Part (a): 'around this time' puts them at about the same time as the cities
Part (b): archaeological evidence and the most ancient Tamil literature

questions.q: A student says, 'Sisupalgarh, with its strict square plan and imposing fortifications, must be a Harappan city, since planned cities are Harappan.' Use the chapter to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter lists Sisupalgarh among the major cities that emerged in the eastern region in the 1st millennium BCE. The Harappan urban order disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE and urban life was largely absent for about a thousand years afterwards, so a 1st-millennium city belongs to the Second Urbanisation, not to the Harappan phase.
s: Sisupalgarh is placed among the cities that emerged in the 1st millennium BCE
The Harappan order disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE, with urban life largely absent for about a millennium
So Sisupalgarh belongs to the Second Urbanisation; being planned does not make it Harappan

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sisupalgarh, now a suburb of Bhubaneswar, is a modern settlement founded after 1948.
Reason (R): Sisupalgarh was first excavated in 1948, and today it is a suburb of Bhubaneswar.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter describes Sisupalgarh as the capital of the Kalinga region in the 1st-millennium BCE developments; 1948 is when it was first excavated, not founded. R is true but does not support A.

questions.q: A merchant at Kaushambi has a cargo of local cloth to sell at a western port for overseas buyers, and wants to bring back goods of the south. Plan his journey using only the chapter: the kinds of road and place he uses on the way to the port; the route he takes from Kaushambi to the south and the hills he crosses; the southern goods he would buy; and one thing the chapter cannot tell you about his journey.
questions.a: To the port he uses a lateral road, which connected other parts of India with the important ports of the western coast, vibrant centres of trade. From Kaushambi he takes the Dakshinapatha, which crossed the Vindhya Range southward. In the south he buys precious or semiprecious stones, gold or spices, for which the south traded profitably within India and overseas. The chapter cannot tell us, for example, how long the journey took, what it cost, or which port he used.
s: Lateral road to a port on the western coast
The port as a vibrant centre of trade
The Dakshinapatha from Kaushambi, crossing the Vindhya Range
Southern goods: stones, gold or spices
Names a limit: durations, costs or the named port are not in the chapter

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas were mahajanapadas of the Ganga plains.
Statement 2: Lateral roads connected other parts of India with important ports on the western and eastern coasts.
Statement 3: Cities in the south emerged only after the mahajanapadas had ceased to exist, with no earlier sign of trade.
Which statements are correct?
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: they were kingdoms that emerged in the south. Statement 3 is false: southern cities began about 400 BCE, before the mahajanapadas ended, and recent excavations claim some signs of earlier commercial activity.

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Dakshinapatha started from Rajagriha, the capital of Magadha, the strongest state.' Which correction fits the chapter?
o: It started at Kaushambi, then the Vatsa capital near Prayagraj, and crossed the Vindhyas south
It started from Takshashila in Gandhara and ran through the Ganga plains to eastern India
It started from Kaushambi, then the capital of Magadha, and ran back northwest towards Gandhara
It started from Rajagriha but crossed the Vindhya Range only after the mahajanapadas had ended
questions.a: The chapter says the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi (near Prayagraj), then a capital of one of the mahajanapadas (the Fig 4.4 caption names it the capital of Vatsa), and crossed the Vindhya Range to proceed south; Rajagriha was Magadha's capital.

questions.q:
Match each piece of evidence in Column I with what it supports in Column II.
Column I: 1. Recent excavations that find signs of trade before 400 BCE  2. The most ancient Tamil literature that names kings  3. A strict square ground plan, fortifications and broad streets  4. Goods and culture reaching Central and Southeast Asia
Column II: a. Southern cities may be older than 400 BCE  b. The southern kingdoms are known from writing as well as from digs  c. A major planned city of the east  d. An interconnected land reaching beyond India
questions.a: The excavations point to older southern commerce; the literature names the southern kings; the square plan and fortifications mark a major eastern city (Sisupalgarh); and the travel of goods and culture beyond India shows the connected land. Swapping the excavations and the literature is the usual slip.

questions.q: A student says, 'The Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha were the only two roads, so a merchant in central India could not reach any port.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: Many lateral roads also joined other parts of India to the ports of both coasts
The two routes ended at the ports, so every merchant reached the coast by one of them
The ports were reached only by rivers, since the chapter names no roads to the coast at all
A merchant in central India could reach only the eastern ports, since the western ones had no roads
questions.a: The chapter names two widely used routes but adds that many lateral roads also connected other parts of India with important ports on the western and eastern coasts, which were vibrant centres of trade.

questions.q: Isha says: 'In this period cities appeared only in the Ganga plains.' Do you agree? Support your answer with two examples.
questions.a: No. Sisupalgarh, the capital of Kalinga, was a major city in the east with a strict square plan. In the south cities began emerging from about 400 BCE.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'only'
Example from the east: Sisupalgarh in Kalinga
Example from the south: cities from about 400 BCE

questions.q: The chapter says southern cities began emerging from about 400 BCE and that the mahajanapadas ceased to exist by 300 or 200 BCE. (a) Work out the smallest and the largest number of years for which southern cities and mahajanapadas could have existed side by side. (b) Why can the chapter not give a single figure?
questions.a: (a) If the mahajanapadas ceased by 300 BCE the overlap was about 400 - 300 = 100 years; if by 200 BCE, about 400 - 200 = 200 years. So between about 100 and 200 years. (b) The dates are given as 'about 400', and as '300 or 200', so they are approximate and the chapter gives a range, not a year.
s: Part (a): 100 years and 200 years
Part (b): the chapter's dates are approximate ('about 400', '300 or 200')

questions.q:
Ravi, a bead-maker at a southern town like Kodumanal near Erode, has 120 ornaments. Merchants from the Ganga plains offer Rs 40 per piece at his workshop. At a western port, buyers for overseas sale would pay Rs 58 per piece, but taking the load there by road costs Rs 1,800.
(a) Work out his money from each choice after costs, and the difference.
(b) The chapter explains why southern goods sell well in both markets. Which resources and which two kinds of buyer does it give?
(c) Which kind of road leads from other parts of India to the western port, and what does the chapter call such ports?
(d) Which choice should Ravi make? Decide using your answers to (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Workshop sale: 120 x 40 = Rs 4,800. Port sale: 120 x 58 = Rs 6,960, less Rs 1,800 = Rs 5,160; the port gives Rs 360 more (7.5 percent). (b) Stones, gold and spices; the rest of India and kingdoms and empires overseas. (c) Lateral roads; vibrant centres of trade. (d) The port: it pays Rs 360 more, and the chapter says ports were vibrant centres of trade and that the south traded profitably overseas; the workshop sale saves effort and the risk of the journey, so a careful answer notes that the gain is small.
s: Part (a): Rs 4,800 and Rs 5,160; difference Rs 360
Part (b): stones, gold, spices; buyers within India and overseas
Part (c): lateral roads; vibrant centres of trade
Part (d): chooses the port, justified by Rs 360 more and the chapter, noting the small gain

questions.q: A guide at a museum holds up a palm-leaf manuscript and says, 'We know about the three southern kingdoms of this period only from writings like this.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: It adds archaeological evidence to the most ancient Tamil literature that names the kings
The chapter says the kingdoms are known only from archaeology, since no writing of that time survives
The chapter says the kingdoms are known from the mahajanapadas' coins and from no writing at all
The chapter agrees, since it names no archaeological site anywhere in the south
questions.a: The chapter says that, apart from archaeological evidence, the most ancient Tamil literature mentions the kingdoms and several of their kings; so the guide's 'only' is too strong. (It also names Kodumanal, an excavated site of shell and gemstone industries.)

questions.q:
Three students plan projects for an exhibition called 'Connected India', whose aim is to show that connections reached beyond India. Karan will build a model of the road that begins at Kaushambi and crosses hills to the south (Rs 40,000). Leela will build a model of Sisupalgarh, the eastern city with a strict square plan, imposing fortifications and broad streets (Rs 55,000). Mohan will show the south, rich in stones, gold and spices, trading profitably within India and overseas (Rs 30,000). The exhibition has Rs 75,000.
(a) List every pair of projects with its cost and say which pairs the fund can pay for.
(b) Which project shows connections beyond India, according to the chapter?
(c) What does Karan's project add to Mohan's?
(d) Decide which projects to fund and say why Leela's is left out.
questions.a: (a) Karan + Leela = Rs 95,000 (no); Karan + Mohan = Rs 70,000 (yes); Leela + Mohan = Rs 85,000 (no). (b) Mohan's, since the south traded with kingdoms and empires overseas. (c) Karan's project adds the Dakshinapatha, the road from Kaushambi across the Vindhya Range to the south, showing how the south was linked by road to the Ganga plains. (d) Fund Karan and Mohan (Rs 70,000, Rs 5,000 left): together they show the road link to the south and its overseas trade. Leela's model is left out because the pair with Mohan costs Rs 85,000, over the fund, and a planned eastern city does not show links beyond India.
s: Part (a): 95,000; 70,000; 85,000; only Karan and Mohan is affordable
Part (b): Mohan's, as the south traded overseas
Part (c): the Dakshinapatha linking the Ganga plains to the south across the Vindhyas
Part (d): funds Karan and Mohan and explains leaving out Leela by cost and aim

questions.q: A student claims: 'The Subcontinent became one interconnected land only because the mahajanapadas united it.' Test the claim against the chapter, giving evidence for and against and a conclusion.
questions.a: The claim fails. The chapter says routes opened for trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns, not only for states; lateral roads linked other regions with the ports; cities and kingdoms emerged in the south with its own resources and trade; and the interconnected land is dated to 300 or 200 BCE, about the time the mahajanapadas ceased to exist. The chapter does say the Uttarapatha ran through the Ganga plains where many mahajanapadas lay, so they may have helped, but it does not say they united the Subcontinent.
s: Routes opened for trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns, not only for states
Lateral roads linked the ports; the south's resources and overseas trade grew separately
The interconnection (300 or 200 BCE) came about the time the mahajanapadas ceased to exist
A point for the claim: the Uttarapatha ran through the Ganga plains where many lay, but 'united it' is not said
A conclusion that the claim goes beyond the chapter
